title: Solar and Reactor Neutrinos: Production, Oscillation and Detection Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Settle in.
paragraphs: Welcome in. I am Professor Harold Vaughn, and this is Solar and Reactor Neutrinos: Production, Oscillation and Detection Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds. This is lesson 1 of 1 in the full thirty-minute build of this class. In this lesson we take the class's own material in order — nothing here is imported, and nothing is asked later that is not taught here first. We begin here: Settle in.

Settle in. I am Professor Harold Vaughn, and this is Solar and Reactor Neutrinos: Production, Oscillation and Detection Budgets Against Density and Energy Bounds. This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

'Borexino Geoneutrinos: Detector Background and Signal Budget with Reactor Antineutrino Background'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): geo_events_expected = 40.4; reactor_events_expected = 68.5; signal_to_reactor_background_ratio = 0.59; signal_significance_approx_sigma = 5.88; total_IBD_rate_TNU = 126.6. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Now we go one step further into the material.

'Daya Bay: The Theta-13 Measurement as a Near-Far Rate Budget'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): deficit_percent = 6.0; far_events_per_day_implied = 611.0; deficit_significance_sigma = 5.45; sin22theta13_from_ratio_adopted_factor = 0.084; far_oscillation_phase_rad = 1.28. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
The next piece is where this starts to come together.

'Gallium Experiments: The pp-Neutrino Capture Budget in Solar Neutrino Units'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): combined_measured_SNU = 67.35; measured_to_predicted_ratio = 0.514; pp_share_of_prediction_percent = 53.2; pp_alone_to_measured_ratio = 1.035; non_pp_predicted_SNU = 61.3; experiment_difference_SNU = 3.9. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Listen carefully here — this piece carries weight in the questions later.

'JUNO: Reactor Antineutrino Event-Rate and Mass-Ordering Sensitivity Budget'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): IBD_events_per_day_raw = 76.1; IBD_events_per_day_detected = 62.4; IBD_events_in_six_years = 136831; mass_ordering_significance_six_years_sigma = 3.18; events_per_day_per_kilotonne = 3.12. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
We take the pieces in order, because each one stands on the last.

'KamLAND Reactor Antineutrinos: Oscillation Survival and Event-Rate Budget'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): events_per_day_no_oscillation = 1.35; events_per_day_with_survival = 0.65; events_per_year_with_survival = 235.8; suppression_percent = 40.0; oscillation_phase_at_mean_energy = 4.293. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Stay with me, because the next piece builds directly on that one.

'Matter-Enhanced Oscillation in the Sun: The MSW Resonance Energy as a Density Budget'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): rho_res_E1MeV_g_cm3 = 289.03; rho_res_E2MeV_g_cm3 = 144.52; rho_res_E5MeV_g_cm3 = 57.81; rho_res_E10MeV_g_cm3 = 28.9; cos2theta12 = 0.3927; resonance_energy_at_centre_MeV = 1.927; pp_survival_approx = 0.577. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take the paper “Borexino Geoneutrinos: Detector Background and Signal Budget with Reactor Antineutrino Background”. Its stated result is: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): geo_events_expected = 40.4; reactor_events_expected = 68.5; signal_to_reactor_background_ratio = 0.59; signal_significance_approx_sigma = 5.88; total_IBD_rate_TNU = 126.6. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong. The worked answer: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

Let us gather what this lesson taught, in order: Settle in; 'Borexino Geoneutrinos: Detector Background and Signal Budget with Reactor Antineutrino Background'; 'Daya Bay: The Theta-13 Measurement as a Near-Far Rate Budget'; 'Gallium Experiments: The pp-Neutrino Capture Budget in Solar Neutrino Units'; 'JUNO: Reactor Antineutrino Event-Rate and Mass-Ordering Sensitivity Budget'; 'KamLAND Reactor Antineutrinos: Oscillation Survival and Event-Rate Budget'. Those are the pieces — hold them in that order, because the questions follow the same road.

That is the lesson, whole. Below it are the questions — every one of them drawn from what was just taught, and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read a piece again is learning, not cheating. When you are ready, begin.

questions.walk: Walk it through with me, step by step. Now it is yours: say that value, in any honest form.
